First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00111

They were asked: “Did you not begin your proof with the existence of a possible thing, something you observe to have been absent before or after it existed?” They answered that the proof needs only one existent thing. If it is necessary, that is the point they seek to prove; if it is possible, then, by the argument just given, it must depend on the Necessary Being.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00112

Some then questioned whether this argument is truly a proof. They said there are only two kinds of proof: one that proceeds from a cause to its effect, and one that proceeds from an effect to its cause. God is not caused by anything; He is the cause of everything else. So any proof of His existence must proceed from an effect, and that kind of proof does not give certainty. They answered that the proof does not begin by pointing to God's own existence, which is the cause of all things. It shows instead that one instance of the shared idea “existent” must be necessary. The fact that the concept “existent” includes a necessary instance is one of the states that follow from it. So the proof moves from a feature of the shared concept to another feature that depends on the first.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00113

Another way they put it was this: they were not proving that the Necessary Being exists in Himself; they were proving that He belongs to the concept “existent.” Avicenna offers a similar example when he argues from the existence of something composed to the existence of what it is composed of. God's existence in Himself is the cause of everything else, but His belonging to this concept is an effect of it. A thing can be a cause in itself and an effect in relation to something else. That is the answer given by some careful thinkers.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00114
But this answer is plainly strained. As we said earlier, the Necessary Being is not proved in Himself, but by something that follows from Him. There is a proof that resembles one from a cause.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00115

Another path that thinkers have praised is supposed to work without disproving circular causes or an endless chain. The author of The Conversations gives it. Suppose that all existence consists only of possible things, whether their chain goes on without end or circles back on itself. Then all possible things together are like one possible thing: they need a cause. That cause must be either the whole itself, one of its members, or something outside it. If the whole caused itself, it would have to come before itself. If one member caused it, that member would have to come before itself and its own causes. If its cause were outside the whole, then, since everything in the whole is possible, what lies outside it can only be the Necessary Being. This argument does not work for us. Existence and oneness go together; in fact, existence itself is one. We have already learned that a collection, simply as a collection, has no existence beyond the existences of its members. A collection of Zayd and Amr is just two people. It is not a third thing that exists outside the mind. So someone may say that all possible things have no cause other than the causes of their individual members. The cause of the collection is just the collection of causes of its members. Those causes are not outside the possible things, since some possible things cause others. So this alone does not require us to reach the Necessary Being.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00116
Only if we also rule out an endless chain could this argument reach the Necessary Being. In that case it would not be a different path after all.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00117

It is surprising that, when this path was challenged with the claim that a thing might cause itself, its defenders answered by saying that the whole made up of the Necessary Being and the first effect is itself possible because it depends on its members. They said it has no cause other than itself: its cause cannot be one of its parts, because it would depend on the rest of them, and nothing lies outside it. So, they concluded, the whole must be its own cause. In answering, they accepted that a thing's complete cause can be the thing itself. They said that if “cause” means all the members on which the whole depends, then the cause is the whole itself.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00118

They said this is no problem, because the whole's dependence on each member does not mean that it depends on the whole, which would make it depend on itself. If “cause” means the acting cause, then one member—the Necessary Being, or something above the last effect and ultimately dependent on the Necessary Being—is its cause. Every member depends on the Necessary Being, so even the possible members of the collection have no effect on the whole apart from the Necessary Being's effect, whether directly or through others.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00119

They did not see that this answer destroys the argument. Their proof depends on saying that the whole cannot be its own complete cause and that one part cannot act as the cause of the whole. The reply says both are possible. It simply gives away the point at issue and tears down the proof.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00120

All this confusion came from assuming that a whole made up of two or more things exists as something apart from the existence of each member. They decided that the whole made up of the Necessary Being and the first effect is a possible thing that needs a cause, then claimed that its complete cause is itself. They forgot that this makes no sense. Every possible thing that exists needs a complete acting cause. A whole made up of all its members can be the same as the whole only in numbers or amounts that the mind groups together by choice, such as an army or a number. Such collections have no reality outside the separate members.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00121

One careful thinker among them answered the problem of a whole made up of the Necessary Being and the first effect by saying that we can consider more than one thing as a single group, or consider the things separately. “The group” names them when considered as one; “this and that” names them when considered separately. These can have different descriptions. A whole crowd cannot fit in a small house if everyone enters at once, but the people can fit if they enter one at a time. Knowing this, we can say that what makes the two things exist together is the two things considered separately. Since the whole depends on both parts, together they are enough to make it exist. So this and that are two causes that make the group exist.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00122

If someone then asks about the two things considered separately, we answer that we do not accept that they are possible when taken that way. In that case they are two things: one necessary existent and one possible existent.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00123

A contemporary thinker rejected this answer. In his example, what exists is the Necessary Being and its effect. Considered together, they form one group; considered separately, there are two. Surely both are real, he says, because a whole disappears only when one of its members disappears, and every member is present. A possible thing must have a cause whether it is one or many, and whether we consider it as a whole or as separate parts. Taking things together or separately changes only how we look at them, not what they are. So the whole made up of the Necessary Being and the first effect exists, whether we consider it as one group or two things. Here “the whole” means the two things that bear the relation of being together, but not the relation itself. This whole exists, even if the relation and the fact that there are two are not themselves things that exist. The one exists in the same way: it exists, though the feature of oneness does not exist as a thing on its own.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00124

If the two things that bear this relation exist, and the whole depends on them, it must have a cause. But there is no other thing that could be its cause. So, the contemporary thinker concludes, this answer does not solve the problem. We say that both replies miss the point. They fail to recognize what existence is: it is not a mental feature added to things, and a thing's existence is its own particular identity. A group does not become one thing in reality just because the mind treats two things as one. The mind's act of grouping them does not give them one nature with a separate rule of its own. What we take together from a human being and a stone is neither a human nor a stone, nor is it some third thing. The same is true of what we group together from a substance and an accident, or from the Necessary Being and a possible being. A number exists outside the mind only in the sense that its individual units exist; the mind can group them together, and in that sense the number has a kind of existence in thought.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00125

The first reply goes wrong in several ways. It assumes that the same thing can be both cause and effect, different only in how we consider it. That is impossible: cause and effect are opposites and cannot belong to the same thing, even under two descriptions. It also says that if the group made up of the Necessary Being and the first effect existed as one possible thing, then the Necessary Being would bring two things into being at the first level: the first effect and the group. But their own teaching says it brings one thing into being, not two. It further says that this combined being is not one of the kinds of existence in their own scheme. It is not the Necessary Being, an intellect, a soul, a body, or an accident. Yet everything that exists must belong to one of these kinds.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00126

At the end of his argument, the first thinker accidentally gives the right answer: if the two things are considered separately, they are two—a necessary being and a possible one. There is no need to group them as one real thing to make the objection apply. Nothing requires them to be one thing in the outside world, and their being together actually shows that they are two.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00127

The second thinker makes some of the same mistakes, and adds another. He argues that a group exists because its members exist, and that it would disappear only if one of its members disappeared. Neither point proves what he wants. The members' existence means that each exists in its own distinct way, for example as necessary or possible, substance or accident. So a group exists only through several distinct existences, with their different rules. And saying that a whole disappears when one of its members disappears does not show that every collection of separate things has one real existence of its own. It applies to a real whole that has one natural form, or could have one. It does not apply to every set of things the mind can group together.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00128

The same mistake would make ordinary divisions useless. If we say that every thing is either necessary or possible, every substance either separate from matter or material, and every word either a noun, verb, or particle, these divisions would not cover everything unless two of the divisions could never each have a real existence of their own.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00129

Among the paths to this goal that do not rely on disproving circular causes or an endless chain is one based on possibility. First, remember that a possible thing does not exist until its existence becomes necessary. And just as a possible thing does not make itself exist, it cannot make its own existence more likely. If it could, it would be enough to bring itself into being and would be necessary in itself, as we have already explained.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00130

The argument is this: no possible thing, whether it is one or many, or whether its members are ordered or equal in rank, can make anything exist necessarily. Whatever makes something necessary must make every way it could fail to exist impossible. But possible things cannot do this. The whole chain of possible causes and effects could cease to exist, even if the effect could not cease while its cause remained—as happens with features that cannot be separated from possible things. So all possible things, whether limited in number or endless, are like one possible thing: they cannot make the absence of their effect impossible, so they cannot make it necessary. For a possible thing to exist, its cause must therefore lie outside the chain of possible things and be the Necessary Being. This is what we wanted to show. This is the point Al-Farabi makes when he says:
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00131

“If a chain of beings existed without necessity, and its first member existed by itself as a possible thing, it would either bring itself into being, which is absurd, or be able to cease by itself, which is even more absurd.”
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00132

In other words, if a possible thing gives itself necessary existence and makes nonexistence impossible, then it would be its own cause, which is false because it would have to come before itself. If it does not make its existence necessary and its nonexistence impossible, then it could cease to exist on its own. That is even more clearly false. The first problem still applies: in some way, the thing would be the cause of itself. The second problem is that if it could cease to exist after it had come into being, then it could even more readily have failed to exist in the first place. So it cannot have come into being without something that made its existence necessary.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00133
Chapter 3 — A Persian Proof, and Its Flaws
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00134

A Persian thinker offered these arguments for the claim that God exists. He said: “If all existing things were only possible, there would have to be a circle of causes. For, on that assumption, the existence of any thing would depend on something being brought into existence, while bringing anything into existence would itself depend on something already existing.”
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00135

He offered another argument: “Existence, considered simply as existence, has no beginning. If it did, it would have to come before itself. This proves that the Necessary Being exists, as is clear with a little thought. This deserves to be called the path of the people of truth, who use the truth itself as their proof. Put another way, all existing things together cannot have a cause in themselves. This proves the Necessary Being. Or again: all existing things together cannot become sheer nothing, while all possible things together could become sheer nothing. This proves the Necessary Being.” That is his argument.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00136

I say that each of these arguments has a flaw. The first does not lead to the kind of circle that thinkers call impossible. A true circle requires the two ends to be the same individual thing. It is not enough for a human being to depend on a seed and for that seed to depend on a human being of the same kind. The mistake is to treat a whole kind as if it were one individual, and to confuse sameness of kind with sameness of the particular thing.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00137

Muhammad al-Shahrastani made a similar mistake in his book The Downfall of the Philosophers. He says that if the world had no beginning in time, there would have to be a circle of causes. The circle between seed and human, or egg and chicken, is broken only if we choose one end as the beginning. Otherwise, each depends on the other, and neither would be more likely to exist than the other. Since they do exist, one must come first. He says the circle must therefore be broken by starting with one of them; in the human line, it is better to start with the more complete form.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00138

The scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi replied: “You have done well in answering what ordinary people and children ask. But this is not a real circle; it is a circle only in words. If a thing depends on something that depends on another thing of the same kind, the result need not be that neither can exist. They may instead form an endless chain. If such a chain is impossible, then it must have a beginning. Here al-Shahrastani has confused a circle with an endless chain.”
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00139

The second argument is also flawed. It leaves out a condition needed for a contradiction: the subject must be the same particular thing. A thing can come before or after itself in a general sense without contradiction, so long as it is not the same individual in both cases. As we explained at the start of this journey, first philosophy studies the most general kinds of things that exist, and the principles of existing things are also features of existence. Avicenna says the same in The Healing.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00140

As for the third argument, if “all existing things” means each one separately, we do not accept that they have no cause. On the assumption being discussed, each thing has a cause. If “all existing things” means the whole group as one, then, as we said, there is no group that exists apart from the many individual things. Just as there is no existence apart from the existences of its members, there is no need for a cause apart from the causes of its members.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00141

The fourth argument shows only that existence as existence differs from possibility as possibility. It is impossible for something that exists, considered simply as existing, to become complete nonexistence. In that claim, the thing is already assumed to exist. But a possible thing, considered apart from its existence, can become nothing in itself. This does not mean that there is some existing thing that is not possible. So the conclusion does not follow from the difference between existence and possibility.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00142

The better way to complete these arguments is to show that an endless chain of causes is impossible. Otherwise, the arguments do not work—unless one can first prove that all possible things form one possible being that needs a cause outside itself. That claim depends on proving that the whole has one unified form and a real nature of its own, unlike a number or a collection of separate things. We have already shown the problem with that claim.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00143
Chapter 4 — Other Arguments That Do Not Hold Up
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00144

The philosophers who study God have another path. They use two kinds of proof. One first shows that God exists, then proves that He is one. The other first proves that the Necessary Being must be one, then shows that bodies, their forms, and their features are many. None of these can be the Necessary Being, so they must be possible and must depend on something that makes them exist.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00145

One way to prove that the bodily world is possible is to note that bodies of different kinds are clearly made up of parts. Each has the shared feature of being a body, and something that makes it one kind of body rather than another. A merely vague body cannot exist. It does not matter whether we accept matter that is more basic than body, or whether we accept a substantial form that gives a body its kind. Even those who reject such forms accept that bodies must have some definite shape or feature to exist at all. Bodies, then, are possible because they are made up of parts. Their forms and features are also possible because they need matter or something in which to exist. On any account, bodies depend on what makes them definite, and those causes depend on what they exist in. Souls also depend on bodies. Neither a body nor a soul can be the cause that makes the other exist, because that would make a thing come before itself. Nor can one body bring another into existence.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00146

As we have explained, a physical thing can affect another only through a shared position in space, and that relation cannot exist until both things exist. Also, the bodies cannot stretch back without end, as the proofs about the limits of size show. So the cause of all bodies must be something that is neither a body nor physical. That is what we wanted to show.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00147

Natural philosophers have other paths, based on change. One begins with motion itself. A moving thing does not start its own motion; it needs another mover. The chain of movers must end at something that does not move, so that there is no circle or endless chain. Because it does not change and has no unrealized potential, this unmoved mover must be the Necessary Being, or one of His aspects, as we explained when discussing the world's beginning.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00148

Natural philosophers also show that the movements of the heavenly bodies come from souls, not from nature alone. A soul acts by choice. So those movements have a goal and aim at the good. They do not move from desire or anger, or to gain a benefit from anything below them, since lower things have no importance to them. Nor is one heavenly body aiming at another, or at the bodies or souls above or below it. If that were the goal, their movements would be alike and the number of bodies would not be limited. So the goal of these movements must be something beyond the physical world.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00149
Nor is that goal a soul. If it exists necessarily, it is the one we seek; if not, it must depend on Him. This is the path of Abraham.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00150

A related argument begins from the fact that changing things are plainly possible and have come to be, and that earthly elements are affected by the heavens. The heavenly bodies cannot all be causes of one another. The one held within the others cannot cause the one that contains it, because it is smaller and lower. The containing body cannot cause what lies within it either, because that would make empty space possible. The stars are nobler than other bodies, and the sun is nobler than the rest. Yet even the sun changes, with its rising and setting, so it needs a mover beyond itself. The mistaken ideas held by some ancient star-worshippers came from misunderstanding the heavenly bodies. This argument shows that they are not the highest goal. Something more complete lies beyond them and moves them, not by direct physical contact or change, but by drawing them through thought and giving them light. This is the Necessary Being, the maker of all.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00151

This argument becomes complete through what we have established: every bodily nature, whether heavenly or earthly, changes in its very being. The heavenly bodies change not only in their features, positions, and arrangements, but in their substance and identity too. The one that changes them and keeps them in being by renewing them at every moment is neither a body nor physical. This is the sense of Abraham's story. As he watched the stars and other heavenly bodies disappear, he saw their very being renewed at each moment, while their lasting heavenly patterns and intelligible forms remained with God.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00152

God says, “In this way We showed Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be among those with certainty.” With his mind, Abraham traveled from this world, which fades and passes away, to the world of God. He said, “I do not love things that disappear. I turn my face toward the One who made the heavens and the earth, turning away from all falsehood. I am not one of those who associate others with God.”
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00153

Natural philosophers also use a path based on knowledge of the soul. It is noble, though it does not reach as high as the path of the people of truth. Here, the seeker is also the way; on the first path, the goal itself is the way, which is nobler. The argument is this: the human soul is beyond the body, yet it begins when the body begins. At first, a soul cannot be distinguished from a body, and the soul cannot move from one body to another, as we will explain later. So the soul is possible and needs a cause that is neither a body nor physical. A body, simply as a body, cannot cause a soul; otherwise, all bodies would have souls. Nor can a bodily power—another soul, a bodily form, or a bodily feature—cause the soul. Such powers act only through a position in space, but there is no spatial position between them and something that has no place.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00154

Also, nothing is brought into existence by something less noble than itself. The soul has a stronger and nobler kind of existence than the other powers of the body. Its maker must therefore be free of matter and body: God, either directly or through one of the beings of His command and word.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00155

Two objections arise. First, if bodily powers can act or be acted on only through a position in space, then no body or bodily feature could receive existence from a cause beyond matter, since no spatial relation can connect a material thing and something beyond matter. Second, if the soul is beyond the body, then the body and its states should have no effect on it.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00156
We answer the first objection by saying that bodies and matter themselves receive existence.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00157

They receive existence from causes beyond matter, but not through any spatial relation to those causes. So the supposed impossibility does not follow. As for the second objection, we say that the soul is not affected by the body as something separate from it, but through its connection to the body. We discuss this fully in our book The Beginning and the Return.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00158

The theologians use a path close to the natural philosophers' argument from motion. Their path begins from the fact that things have come to be. They say that bodies are never free from motion or rest, and both have come to be. Anything that is never free from things that have come to be must itself have come to be. So all bodies began to exist, and everything that began to exist needs a maker. Their maker must be neither a body nor physical, to avoid a circle or an endless chain. That maker is God.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00159

This is also a good path. We have shown that changes in motion come from changes in the very being of the things that move. Anything that can change must be indefinite and able to receive new substantial forms; its features change because its substance changes. So the bodily world and everything in it fades and passes away at every moment and needs something beyond itself.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00160

The familiar objection to the main premise—that something which is never free of changing things must itself have begun to exist—has already been answered by what we have explained. The other familiar objection says that each movement or moving thing could begin while its kind continues to exist. This objection also fails. A general kind does not exist as a lasting thing in itself, either for those who raise the objection or for us. An essence or idea does not exist on its own; it exists only through particular beings. No motion or moving thing remains the same, in its actual existence and identity, while passing through all these changes.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00161
Chapter 5 — Why God's Existence Is Not Separate from What He Is
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00162

A common proof that God's existence is His very essence goes like this. If an essence has existence, it needs something to make it exist and count as real. Every feature that is not part of a thing's essence must be explained either by the thing itself or by something else. But an essence cannot cause its own existence or make existence necessary for itself. Whatever causes a thing to exist must already exist before it does. If an essence caused its own existence, it would have to exist before it existed, which is impossible. This differs from an essence requiring features other than existence, as a triangle requires three angles and four requires evenness. In those cases, the essence does not have to exist before the feature follows from it. So if God's existence were something added to His essence, it would need a cause outside Him. That is impossible.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00163

We do not think this proof is complete. It also applies to the essences of possible things. Just as an acting cause must exist before its effect, the thing that receives or bears an effect must also be there first.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00164

If someone answers that there is no real receiving of existence by an essence, but only a difference in how the mind considers things—first thinking of an essence without considering existence, then describing it as existing—we can give the same answer if God is said to have an essence. We have also shown that, for anything whose reality is existence, what is real is its existence, not its essence. If existence is brought about by another, then the essence follows from that act of bringing existence about. If existence is not brought about, then neither is the essence. In short, the proof confuses a feature of an essence with a feature of existence. Saying that existence belongs to an essence means only that they differ in the mind's concepts while being one thing in reality.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00165

The proof is sometimes given this way: if God's existence were something added to His essence, then, considered without that added existence, He would be neither existent nor nonexistent, as we explained when discussing essences. Anything like that is possible. If His essence made Him exist, that would be impossible, since something cannot exist before it exists. If something else made Him exist, He would be caused, not necessary. So He would be possible, not necessary.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00166

I say there is another option. His existence could be due to existence itself, just as prime matter has its form because of the form. The form makes matter real and makes it a bearer of that form; nothing else needs to do this. Also, it is not true that every feature a thing has must depend on the thing in the same way. That does not apply to features the mind finds by analyzing an idea.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00167

Someone arguing in the usual way could also say that a cause is needed only for what is possible, as the common view holds. If it is possible for a thing to have a feature or not have it, then something must make it have that feature, as something must make a body white. But if having that feature is necessary or impossible, no cause is needed. The Necessary Being's existence is necessary, so it needs no cause. The source of this necessity is existence itself, not an essence. When people say that the Necessary Being's essence requires existence, they mean only that it cannot fail to exist. They do not mean that its essence acts on existence. One careful thinker therefore says that God's attributes are not effects He produces.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00168

People also say that, for us, necessity means that a thing requires existence. If God's essence requires existence, does that not make His essence the cause of His existence? The answer given by a later thinker is that there is no difference between causing and requiring, except in the words. If God's essence requires existence, then it causes its own existence. If “requiring” only means that it cannot fail to exist, then either this impossibility comes from the essence itself, which makes the essence a cause, or it comes from something else, which means God depends on that other thing and is not necessary.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00169

I say someone can offer another answer: perhaps the impossibility of not existing comes from existence itself. Existence requires that God have an essence that exists through it, just as a species requires a broader kind. The idea “animal” is different from the ideas “rational” and “human.” If we consider animal by itself, it may be rational or not, human or not. But if we consider what it means to be human as the essence, and what it means to be rational as its actual existence, then being an animal is necessary for being human. Saying that a human being requires animal nature means only that a human being, so long as it is human, is an animal. Likewise, saying that rational existence requires animal nature does not mean there are two existences or an act of causing between them. Being rational is itself being an animal, without one coming before the other.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00170

The broader kind and the difference are one in reality, though their meanings differ. If we considered animal without rationality and rationality without animal nature, then they would have different existences. But the mind invents that separation; it has no basis in reality. What these thinkers say would make sense only for those who treat existence as a mental idea and treat the essences of things as what truly exists. They say that existence is a general mental idea, not something real in itself. For them, the essence of a possible thing cannot be called existent unless something else makes it so; but God's essence, if it were present in the mind, would itself be enough for the mind to call it existent. The learned Dawani states this view directly: the shared general idea of existence is a second-order concept, not the real identity of any thing. The mind adds it to every thing, but in possible beings it arises from their being made by another, while in God it arises from His own being.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00171
For that view, God exists through Himself. If the mind considers Him, it draws from Him the general idea of existence, unlike anything else. That is the end of the argument.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00172

Their way of speaking shows that, for them, saying “existence is the same as God's essence” is only a special use of words. They do not mean that God is a real instance of existence. Their claim applies only to the general mental idea of existence, not to the reality of existence that makes each thing real. On our view, each thing's existence is what is real in it. Existence is not added to one thing and identical to another in the same way. When we say that existence is added to a possible thing but identical with God, we mean that a possible thing is not real if we ignore the one who gives and sustains it. A caused thing depends on what brings it into being. Its existence comes from a direct act of creation, and its cause upholds it. If we set aside its cause, its existence is no longer real. The Necessary Being, by contrast, exists through Himself, not through anything else. A possible thing cannot be complete without the Necessary Being. God's existence completes everything else; He is independent of all that exists beyond Him. In this sense, existence is added to what is possible but is the very reality of the Necessary Being. Consider this carefully; it deserves to be believed.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00173

There is another way to understand the statement that possible things have an essence while the Necessary Being has none. Every being other than the Necessary Being can be considered at a level of reality where it does not yet exist through its own particular existence. At that level, we can imagine its essence as not yet existing and as a known form. A body, simply as a body, does not exist at the level of the soul. The soul, simply as a soul, does not exist in the world of intellect. Likewise, something made by another does not have its own existence at the level of its maker. So its essence can be considered there before it has this particular existence. The first principles can know the forms of things before the things themselves exist.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00174

The Necessary Being is different. He exists in Himself and at every level of existence. This does not mean He becomes different things at different times. It means that there is no part of the world where it is not true that God exists, and no aspect of existence in which He has no place.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00175

Here is another argument that the Necessary Being has no essence. If existence were added to an essence, that essence would have to belong to one of the basic kinds of thing. It would have to be a substance, not one of the features that depend on something else, because those features can exist only in a subject. But if it belonged to the kind of substance, it would need a further feature to distinguish it from other kinds of substance, and so it would need something to make it distinct.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00176

Some kinds of substance clearly need such a distinguisher. And if a possibility belongs to any kind under a general class, then it also belongs to the class itself. If possibility did not apply to the general class, it could not apply to any kind beneath it. For example, if “animal” could not possibly be “stone,” then no kind of animal could be a stone. Whatever is impossible or necessary for the general class by itself also applies to its kinds.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00177

So if the Necessary Being belonged to one of these classes, the class would make Him possible in some respect. He would no longer be necessary, which is impossible. Since the Necessary Being cannot belong to a class, He cannot have an essence in this sense. He is pure existence. This is what we wanted to show.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00178
Chapter 6 — God's Oneness: He Has No Partner in Necessary Existence
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00179

We have already given a special proof from the highest level of insight. No one before us had noticed it. We set it out in the first part, on universal knowledge and the rules that govern existence. Here we will point to another noble proof that begins from much the same place.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00180

The familiar proof goes like this. If there were more than one being that exists necessarily, each would have to differ from the other. Either each would differ through its own essence, or through something added to its essence. If they differed through their own essences, then the concept “necessary being” would apply to each only as an attribute. But every attribute depends on what it describes. Each would then be the cause of its own necessary existence, which has already been shown impossible.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00181

If they differed through something added to their essences, that added feature would either be caused by their essences or by something else. The first is impossible. If their essences were one, their individual identities would also be one, so there would be no plurality of either essence or identity—contrary to what we assumed. If their essences were different, necessary existence, or existence at its fullest strength, would be an attribute added to them. We have already shown that God's existence is not added to His essence. If something else caused their difference, each would depend on something else to be the individual it is. Anything that depends on another for its identity also depends on it for its existence. It would therefore be possible, not necessary.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00182

The reply is that the claim “necessary existence is identical with God's essence” cannot mean that the familiar idea of necessary existence is His essence. No reasonable person would say that. If instead it means that God's essence is itself the source from which the concept of existence is drawn, while a possible thing's essence cannot by itself give rise to that concept, why could there not be two things, each of which is in itself the source of the concept and the reality it describes?
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00183

A defender of the proof might answer that what gives rise to the shared concept of existence must be a particular existence; and that existence, together with the identity it gives rise to, cannot be something added to the thing's essence. So a particular, necessary existence is identical with its own individual reality and cannot be shared or multiplied. But this leads to the famous objection attributed to Ibn Kamuna: at first glance, the intellect does not rule out two simple identities, each of which cannot be divided into essence and existence, each existing simply through itself and needing no cause. This is why people have said that the philosophers' argument here equivocates between a concept and a particular instance. When they said God's existence is identical with His essence, they meant the real existence that subsists through itself. But when they argued that existence cannot be shared because it is identical with His essence, they meant the concept of existence.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00184

If they meant the particular existence that subsists through itself, their proof of oneness would not follow. There could be two particular existences, each subsisting through itself and distinguished by its own essence. Each would be a particular existence, distinct in itself, and its individual existence would be identical with its essence, just as the philosophers say when there is only one.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00185

I say that this objection has great force against later thinkers who treat existence as only a mental idea. For them, what all existents share is only a general concept drawn from them; the shared concept has no real instance, either in God or in possible things. When they call God's existence “particular,” that is only a special use of the word.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00186

But on the view we have established, the general concept of existence has real instances. It relates to them as a broad feature relates to the particular things it describes. The objection is therefore much weaker and can be answered with a little care. Although the concept is drawn from an essence because of some feature, it is drawn from every particular existence because of what that existence is in itself. Its relation to particular existences is like the relation of meanings such as “humanity” to a human being or “animality” to an animal. We have seen that a shared meaning follows from what the things it is drawn from have in common. Its having one meaning follows from the unity of its sources, and its having many instances follows from their plurality.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00187

For example, the one concept “humanity” is drawn from every human being, but not from a horse, a cow, or any other kind of thing. So the fact that one concept applies to several things means that what it describes is in some way shared by them, whether that shared feature is a broader kind or a species. If there were two beings that each existed necessarily, the concept of existence would be shared between them, as even the objector admits. The real existence from which the concept is drawn would also have to be shared in some way. They would therefore have to differ from each other in their basic essences. When two things share something essential, their difference must also be essential. Neither could then be simple, and this kind of composition is incompatible with necessary existence.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00188

One issue remains. The feature that distinguishes two things can sometimes be the same feature they share, as when one thing has more or less of a quality than another. We see this in the reality of existence. Someone could therefore say that one necessary being differs from another because its existence is more complete and stronger, while both remain simple in themselves. At first glance, we have no proof that one necessary being cannot be less complete than another, even if we agree that it cannot be less complete than a possible being.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00189

This objection can be answered by what we said earlier: any lack implies that a thing is caused. The reality of existence cannot be incomplete in itself, without a cause. Lack is not the same as existence; it is an absence. A thing cannot give rise to its own absence. Perfection, by contrast, strengthens what a thing already is. A longer line is longer through the nature of line itself. But we cannot say that a shorter line is shorter because of the nature of line; it is shorter because it lacks some length. Any line that is unlimited has nothing in it but the nature of line. A limited line has both line and something else: an endpoint or boundary that line itself does not require. So any existence that is limited in strength must have a cause, other than that particular existence, that sets and establishes its degree. Being caused is incompatible with necessary existence, which means existing eternally by itself. There cannot, then, be more than one necessary being.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00190

This argument, in this form, does not work on the view that existence is only a mental idea. But we can restate it this way: the general concept of existence has one shared meaning among all existents. The source of that concept in possible things is not their essences by themselves, but their relation to the One who gives and sustains them. In the Necessary Being, the source of the concept is His essence itself. In reality, then, it is God's essence that is the source of the concept of existence in every case. If there were more than one Necessary Being, each would, by its own essence, be an instance of this one shared meaning and the source from which it is drawn. Yet common sense tells us that one shared meaning cannot belong to completely different things only because they differ. There must be some common feature among them. So the two necessary beings would share an essential feature outside either one, and they would also have to differ through another feature of their essences, as a species differs from another species by its defining feature, or one individual differs from another by its individual mark. This composition is incompatible with necessary existence. This gives a sound basis for the proofs the philosophers offered.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00191

One such proof appears in Avicenna's Annotations: “The existence of the Necessary Being is identical with His individual reality. So being existent is the same as being Himself. The Necessary Being does not exist for the sake of something else.” On our account, this cannot be challenged by asking why there could not be two things, each with its own particular existence identical to its own reality. If “being Himself” means that His particular existence is identical with Him, the same could be said of two things. If it means that His being existent in general is identical with Him, that is not accepted, since the shared meaning of existence requires the real source of existence to be shared as well.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00192

Another proof says: if more than one Necessary Being existed, they would either have the same essence or different essences. If they had the same essence, that essence could not by itself apply to many individuals; otherwise many things would exist without the one that makes them one. If their essences differed, then necessary existence would be an attribute added to each. Every added attribute depends either on the thing that bears it or on something else. Both options fail. If it depended on its bearer alone, each would cause its own existence. If it depended on something else, the problem would be even worse. This proof too can face the familiar objection, despite the premise just explained.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00193

Another proof comes from al-Farabi in Fusus: “Necessary existence cannot be divided so that it applies to many things that differ in number; otherwise it would be caused.” The brief statement sums up the argument we have given. It is a short proof that avoids Ibn Kamuna's objection, because that objection depends on treating existence as only a general concept, as the Illuminationist philosopher and most later thinkers did. Suhrawardi himself raised the objection directly in al-Muṭāraḥāt and hinted at it in al-Talwīḥāt. Ibn Kamuna, one of the commentators on Suhrawardi, later repeated it in one of his works, and it became known by his name. Because he strongly held that existence is only a mental idea and has no reality outside the mind, he wrote in one of his books: “The arguments they give show only that there cannot be more than one Necessary Being with the same essence. If their essences differ, another proof is needed, and I have not found one so far.”
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00194
Chapter 7 — A Later Thinker’s Proof of Oneness, and Its Problems
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00195
The learned Dawānī says in one of his letters and in his commentary on The Luminous Temples that we should begin with two points.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00196

First, we cannot work out philosophical truths from everyday uses of words. Ordinary speech sometimes uses a word in a way that does not fit what reason shows. For example, people hear the word “knowledge” and think of knowing or learning, which they describe as a relation between things. But philosophical inquiry shows that the form of knowledge may itself be a substance, as when we know a substance, or may exist in itself, as when immaterial beings know themselves, or may even exist necessarily, as when the Necessary Being knows Himself. In the same way, the defining features of substances are often expressed by words that sound like relations or added qualities. “Rational,” for example, is the defining feature of a human being; “sensing” and “moving by choice” define an animal. In truth, these are not relations or added qualities, because any part of a substance must itself be a substance.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00197

Second, a word formed from a quality does not always mean that the quality itself is present in the thing, even if ordinary speech suggests it does. We call Zayd a blacksmith because iron is the material of his work, and call water “sun-heated” because it was warmed by the sun. Dawānī then says that existence, from which we form the word “existent,” might itself be something that exists through itself: the reality of God. Everything else would exist through its connection to Him. The word “existent” would then apply both to that reality and to other things through their relation to it. This broad concept would be a mental construct, one of the second-order ideas, and the first thing we know without proof.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00198
You might ask: how can this reality exist if it is existence itself? And how can “existent” mean more than this one reality?
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00199

Dawānī replies that “existent” does not have to mean something separate from existence, as ordinary usage may suggest. In Persian, it means “is” or “exists.” If we suppose that existence stands by itself, separate from everything else, then it exists through itself and is both existence and existent. In the same way, if a knowing form exists by itself, it knows itself and is knowledge, knower, and known. If heat were separate from fire and existed by itself, it would be both hot and heat. Bahmanyār says in The Book of Joy and Happiness that a sensible form, if separated from the senses and existing by itself, would both sense and be sensed.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00200

Dawānī also says that we know existence is different from what exists when we see that some things can exist and later cease to exist. If they were existence itself, they would have to exist necessarily. Since some existents are not necessary, existence must be something added to them.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00201

You might then ask how this broader meaning is possible. Dawānī answers that it may mean either existence itself or something connected to it in a particular way. The test is whether it is the source of effects. Or the general meaning may be what existence belongs to: either existence standing by itself, where it belongs to itself, or a mental relation that applies to its subjects, as with “universal” and “particular.” Even if “belongs to” is only a figurative way to speak in the first case, it does not follow that “existent” is figurative.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00202

In short, the existence from which we form “existent” is one reality that exists through itself. “Existent” applies both to it and to things related to it. If we read the philosophers this way, we avoid saying that existence as a concept is the first thing we know, while applying it to the self-subsisting reality only as a figure of speech or by a different use of the word. This also clears up the confusion that troubles people who study the question.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00203

You might object that showing how the philosophers’ words could be read this way is not enough. We need proof that this is how things really are. Dawānī answers: proof has shown that the existence of the Necessary Being is identical with His essence, and it is clear that a general idea shared by many things cannot be identical with His essence.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00204

You might then ask why there cannot be two distinct realities, each necessary in itself, with the concept of necessary existence applying to both only as an added quality. Dawānī says that the earlier and later points are enough to answer this. If the concept were an added quality to each, it would be caused either by each thing’s own essence—so that it would have to exist before itself—or by something else, which is worse. It has been established that anything whose necessity or existence is an added quality is possible, not necessary. So the Necessary Being is existence itself, existing in itself at its fullest strength. When we say that the Necessary Being is existent, we mean this. We do not mean that existence is a quality added to a subject. Dawānī says that al-Farabi and Avicenna also held that calling God “existent” is figurative, despite what the word may suggest in ordinary speech.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00205

If this is understood, there cannot be two self-subsisting realities, each necessary in itself, since then necessary existence would be a shared attribute that belonged to both. We can put Dawānī’s point another way. We may begin with the shared meaning of existence and, by examining it, discover that it is not shared as a quality added to different subjects. It is shared because different things are related to one reality. The existence to which all essences are related is something that exists through itself, not a quality added to something else, and is necessary in itself.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00206

At first, we might think that all blacksmiths share iron, and everything warmed by the sun shares the sun. Then we notice that they do not share iron or the sun as qualities present in them; rather, they are related to iron or to the sun. In the same way, what we thought was a shared quality is actually one reality that exists through itself, with other things related to it. There are not many suns or many kinds of iron behind these words.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00207

Dawānī says that the familiar view—that existence is a quality added to essences—raises serious problems. If a thing has a quality, it must already exist in itself. But the subject here is unrestricted existence, and an essence has no existence before unrestricted existence is added to it. Some say that the essence is qualified by existence only in the mind. But this does not help: the question then becomes how it is qualified by mental existence. Making an exception for existence from the rule that a subject must exist before its quality is added to it is arbitrary, especially since leading philosophers have challenged that exception.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00208

He adds that if existence is a quality of essence, and the agent’s effect is to make essence exist, then what the agent first produces must be the relation of essence to existence. But a relation requires the things it relates to exist first. So that relation cannot be the first thing produced. These are some of the problems that arise from saying that existence is a quality added to essences. On Dawānī’s account, none of them arise.
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00209

This is the view Dawānī supports. I say that, although this skilled thinker explained it at length, and most later scholars accepted or even admired it, it does not help with the question of oneness, even if all its premises are sound. Here are several objections. First, we do not accept that the word “blacksmith” is derived from the word “iron.” Iron is a basic noun, not a source from which another word is formed. The same applies to “sun-heated.”
First Discussion — The One Who Must Exist: His manner of existence, perfect oneness, and completeness
passage-en-00210

Second, even if using a derived word for something does not mean that its source quality is present in it, as Dawānī says, the source quality must at least be real in it. His examples of the blacksmith and sun-heated water do not prove otherwise. Those uses may simply be figurative. The source of the word could be “being ironlike” or “being sunlike,” not iron or the sun themselves. We might say the blacksmith has a share in iron because he works with it so much that its image fills his mind. Iron itself cannot exist inside another thing, but an image of iron can exist in the mind. Likewise, we might figuratively call warmed water “sun-heated” because it seems to contain a share of the sun. In short, as Dawānī himself says, we cannot discover the truth from such everyday uses of words. Why rely on them here?
